analysis.one_liner: Caps the total compliance cost of federal regulations through an annual "regulatory budget" that counts only costs, not benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to five House committees and one subcommittee, never received a markup or a floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Congressional Budget Act to create a "regulatory budget": each year Congress would set a dollar ceiling on the total cost private companies, states, and localities incur complying with federal regulations [S3]. Any new rule that would push compliance costs above the cap could not be enforced, because agencies would be barred from spending money on it — a barrier that could only be waived by three-fifths of the chamber [S3]. The cap counts only what compliance costs regulated parties; the value of cleaner air, safer workplaces, safer food, or protected savings is explicitly excluded from the calculation [S3]. It would also force agencies to go through full notice-and-comment rulemaking before issuing major guidance documents, and let anyone sue over guidance or rules issued outside the process [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — manufacturers, energy producers, chemical companies, financial firms, and any business facing federal compliance obligations — would gain a hard ceiling on the total cost of new rules, and a new private right of action to sue agencies over rules and guidance issued outside the required process. Small businesses would get more detailed cost analysis of proposed rules before they take effect [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing federal compliance costs

how_it_helps.text: Creates an annual ceiling on the total cost private sector, states, and localities bear complying with federal regulations, set in the congressional budget resolution, with allocations by committee and agency [S3].

Bars agencies from spending money to enforce any new rule that would breach the regulatory cost cap; the enforcement ban can only be avoided by a vote of three-fifths of the chamber, a threshold higher than a simple majority [S3].

Requires the cost calculation to exclude the value of any benefit a regulation provides, so a rule's usefulness to the public is not weighed against its cost in deciding whether it can be enforced [S3].

Requires major agency guidance documents to go through the same notice-and-comment process as formal rules, and gives anyone aggrieved by unapproved guidance or an unenforceable rule the right to sue in federal court [S3].

Requires agencies to quantify and disclose the monetary compliance costs their proposed rules impose on small entities, other businesses, and individuals, and to analyze costs and benefits industry by industry [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on people who rely on federal protections. Because the cap counts only compliance costs and excludes benefits, rules protecting health, safety, the environment, wages, and consumers would face a hard fiscal ceiling, and once the cap binds, new protections could only move forward by cutting old ones — or not at all. Agencies would lose the ability to use guidance documents, a faster and more flexible tool, to respond to emerging problems [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal health, safety, and environmental rules

drawbacks.text: The regulatory cost definition explicitly excludes the value of any benefit under a regulation, so the cap ignores what the public gets back — cleaner air, safer drugs, protected bank deposits — and counts only what regulated companies spend [S3].

Because the cap is a hard ceiling on total compliance cost, any new protection would have to be paid for by eliminating or weakening an existing one; the bill also lets the President unilaterally set the proposed cost level during the transition period and lets agencies shift costs off the books through emergency, criminal-enforcement, and national-security exemptions [S3].

Supporters would acknowledge the cap is enforced through funding prohibitions and supermajority point-of-order waivers that could parole routine rulemaking into prolonged budget fights, and the private right of action invites litigation against nearly any agency action [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give businesses real cost certainty and force agencies to state compliance costs in numbers, which has genuine value for small firms. But the design is lopsided by construction: it counts only what regulated parties spend and excludes what the public gains, so once the cap binds, health, safety, environmental, and consumer rules would be treated purely as costs to be minimized. For most households, the protections those rules provide are worth more than the cap allows; the bill's benefit to the public is indirect and speculative, while the constraint on protections is direct and automatic.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the House referred it to five committees on the day it was introduced, one later sent it to a subcommittee, and no committee ever marked it up or brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Good (R-VA) introduced the bill on April 15, 2021, with Reps. Mace and Weber of Texas as original cosponsors [S1][S3].

The same day, the Speaker referred it to five committees — Budget, Rules, Judiciary, Oversight and Reform, and Small Business — a multi-committee referral that often signals a bill's prospects are limited [S1][S5].
Six months later, in October 2021, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law; that was the last action of record [S5].
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agencies' ability to issue health, safety, environmental, and financial rules was left intact, and the public keeps the full set of protections the bill would have capped. The bill's backers gained nothing from its failure; regulated industries' compliance obligations remain as they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal regulators and existing public protections

industries.industry: Regulated industries generally (manufacturing, energy, chemicals, finance)
industries.note: The bill would cap their total compliance costs at an annual ceiling and bar enforcement of any rule that breaches it, while excluding regulatory benefits from the calculation. Their gain comes directly from limiting health, safety, environmental, and consumer rules that protect the public.

The bill requires agencies to quantify compliance costs for small entities in specific numbers and analyze industry-by-industry cost impacts, giving small firms more visibility before rules take effect. It does not exempt them from the underlying rules, though.

Agencies would need OMB clearance to enforce any rule that raises measured compliance costs, would lose the ability to issue major guidance documents without full rulemaking, and would face lawsuits over procedural missteps. Their loss of flexibility is also the public's loss of faster regulatory response.
